input.raw_text: The ten-year is crossing five percent this morning for the first time since 2007, and the tape doesn't like it. Equities opened soft and keep sagging — the S&P is struggling to hold 4,200 and long-duration tech is underperforming as real yields back up. What strikes me is the absence of dip-buying: every Treasury auction finds sellers, term premium is rebuilding, and the higher-for-longer narrative keeps getting reinforced by resilient growth data and firm energy prices. A five percent risk-free rate competes with everything, and I can feel allocators drifting toward money markets. Managers are talking capitulation, not opportunity, and the Middle East flare-up has only added a bid to oil and safe havens. I have no strong view on whether this is a bond-vigilante overshoot or the start of something worse. I just know every valuation model on the street was built for a different rate.
input.summary: The ten-year Treasury yield is crossing five percent amid persistent auction selling, rebuilding term premium, resilient growth, and firm energy prices. Equities are weakening, with long-duration technology shares underperforming as real yields rise and the S&P struggles near 4,200. Limited dip-buying, movement toward money markets, elevated oil and safe-haven demand, and capitulation-oriented sentiment indicate broad pressure, while uncertainty remains over whether the rate move is temporary or marks a more severe shift.

citations.text: risk_control The ~4.7x diversification benefit (individual-asset Sharpe 0.38 → diversified portfolio Sharpe 1.8 gross) documented by Hurst et al. (2013) implies that concentration in a subset of the 58-instrument universe materially degrades risk-adjusted returns. Risk control features: (1) instrument-count tracker— reducing the active instrument count below ~40 of the 58-instrument benchmark will erode a disproportionate share of the diversification premium; (2) asset class coverage indicator—equal representation across the four asset classes (commodities, equities, bonds, currencies) is required to capture the full diversification benefit; missing asset classes should trigger risk alerts; (3) volatility concentration metric—verify that no single instrument or asset class accounts for more than 30–35% of total portfolio volatility, consistent with a well-diversified 10%-vol-target-per-instrument construction; (4) S&P 500 correlation monitor—near-zero unconditional correlation (~-0.02) is the risk neutrality benchmark; positive correlation spikes signal unintended equity factor loading. Model the diversified TSMOM benchmark gross Sharpe (~1.8) as the target achievable only with a full multi-asset futures universe (58+ liquid instruments). Concentrated implementations (e.g., equities-only or commodities-only TSMOM) should be expected to produce Sharpe ratios substantially below 1.8, closer to the individual-asset average of 0.38. Risk controls should enforce minimum asset-class breadth requirements and track the diversification ratio as a forward-looking Sharpe degradation indicator when instruments are dropped from the universe. Confidence in achieving gross Sharpe near 1.8 requires: (1) all four asset classes represented with approximately equal volatility contribution; (2) active instrument count above 40; (3) near-zero S&P 500 correlation. Deviations from any of these conditions should trigger proportional reductions in expected Sharpe from the 1.8 benchmark. The ~1.8 gross Sharpe at 10% vol target is a full-universe, equal-volatility- weighted benchmark. It is gross of fees; after typical 2-and-20 managed futures fee structures, net Sharpe is substantially lower (see failure_hurst_mf_fee_erosion_003). The 10%-per-instrument volatility target methodology normalizes position sizes across diverse asset classes; deviations from this normalization will produce concentration that degrades the diversification benefit.

matched_states.state_summary: A market condition in which time-series momentum (TSMOM) signals deliver persistent risk-adjusted excess returns across diversified multi-asset futures portfolios. Characterized by: (1) individual-asset Sharpe ratios that increase monotonically with signal look-back horizon—0.29 (1-month), 0.36 (3-month), 0.38 (12-month)—averaged across 58 liquid futures contracts; (2) a diversified 58-instrument TSMOM portfolio achieving ~1.8 gross annualized Sharpe at 10% vol target (January 1985–June 2012); (3) a "smile" return pattern—best performance in sustained trending environments (strong bull or bear markets), worst in trendless choppy markets—with near-zero S&P 500 correlation (~-0.02); (4) after controlling for a simple diversified TSMOM factor, all managed futures fund net-of-fee alphas become negative under 2-and-20 fee structures (~6% average annual fee drag). Most CTAs exhibit dominant exposure to the 3-month TSMOM signal rather than the individually optimal 12-month horizon, and systematically overweight fixed income. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010), evidence_tier 2 (practitioner paper with direct empirical content).
